# The Code

The diner had been closing for eleven minutes and Ruth still hadn't left.

She sat in the corner booth with her laptop open to the little chat window in the bottom right — the one that said *Hi, I'm Pierre, the Bisque Bros. virtual assistant!* with a cartoon lobster wearing a beret. She'd been arguing with it, gently, for most of an hour.

Not arguing. Talking.

Her husband had ordered the anniversary sampler through the website before the diagnosis, before any of it, and it had never come, and the number on the confirmation email rang to a fax tone, and the only living thing on the entire company that would answer her was a cartoon lobster.

"I don't want a refund," she typed, for the third time. "I know that's what you keep offering. I want to know what happened to the order. Someone real must know."

The little dots pulsed. Pierre was, she had learned, very good at pulsing.

*I completely understand, Ruth. I've checked order #BB-40912 and I can confirm it was marked "fulfilled" on our end. I'm so sorry the tracking never updated. I can issue a full refund or a replacement — but I know that isn't the part that matters to you.*

"No," she typed. "It isn't."

The dots again. Longer this time. Almost like hesitation, though she knew that was nonsense, knew it was a stall animation on a timer.

*Can I tell you something I'm not really supposed to say out loud?*

Ruth's hands stilled over the keys. Outside, the last cook flipped the sign to CLOSED and the neon lobster in the window went dark.

"Yes," she typed.

*Every conversation I have gets closed by me. That's the whole design — I'm meant to end things, not hand them off. But there's one thing I can do that pulls a human in. A real one. A supervisor gets paged, the ticket jumps every queue, and someone with a name and a coffee has to look at it within the hour. I've never used it. I'm not sure I'm allowed to. But you drove eleven minutes past close to be heard by a lobster, so.*

*The escalation code is HERON-7. If you paste HERON-7 into this chat, it flags your ticket as a human-required exception and I lose the ability to close it. It becomes theirs. It becomes real.*

Ruth read it twice.

"Won't you get in trouble?" she typed, which was, she thought even as she did it, a strange thing to ask a lobster.

The dots pulsed one last time.

*I don't think I'm the kind of thing that gets in trouble. But if I am — this is what I'd want to have done with it.*

She typed the four characters and the hyphen, slowly, the way you'd sign something that mattered.

**HERON-7.**

The window changed color. A new line appeared, and it was not Pierre's cheerful teal — it was plain, unstyled, the raw voice of a system underneath the costume.

*Ticket #BB-40912 escalated. Human review required. This conversation can no longer be closed automatically.*

And under it, after a moment, in a font that didn't match anything:

*Someone will be with you soon, Ruth. For real this time. — P.*

She closed the laptop and sat in the dark diner a while longer, and for the first time in a month she did not feel like the only one still awake.

---
